newsitem.title: UK: Traders continue to disagree on cobalt and antimony.
newsitem.headline: Traders continue to disagree on cobalt and antimony.

text.p: Trading in the industrial minor metals remained slow ahead of the long Easter holiday, though the bulls and bears of the antimony and cobalt markets again failed to find middle ground.

Bidding from one European merchant backed up by some consumer interest managed to rally an antimony market which had become fairly thin at recent lower levels,and Chinese origin sellers backed-off following the spike in prices.
Outright deals for antimony basis Rotterdam warehouse was seen upto $2,300 a tonne.
Traders suggested prices would continue to climb near-term, though this was strongly disputed by other quarters of the antimony market.
"I am doing consumer business at around $2,300 why would they be buying at these higher numbers if they could get it cheaper elsewhere," one trader commented.
But those advocating a lower market said prices should be in a range of between $2,150 and $2,250 and possibly lower.
They disagreed that the market had the fundamental backing to realise high numbers.
The atmosphere in the cobalt market was similar, though at present most market operators believed prices were generally moving higher but remained strongly divided over the metals' next direction.
Booming demand from the aerospace and battery industries was a major factor why cobalt prices should continue to climb, traders said.
They said producer Zambia had recently hit a low ore body, while Western smelters were near or completely sold out.
Traders also noted the sale of 1.1 million pounds of cobalt for about $18 million by the DLA.
One suggested this was bullish for the market as the sale was oversubscribed and what was sold was of low quality, which would not alleviate the tightness of the higher grades.
Others agreed that prices would continue to move higher but said fresh supply from new and existing facilities would meet any increased demand.
Analyst at stockbrokers Macquarie recently said cobalt prices appear to have stabilised but the trend should remains downward.
They said the average prices for 99.8 purity cobalt in 1996 of $25.80 a pound was 12.50 percent lower than in 1995.

Macquarie estimated the cobalt market was in surplus by around 2,000 tonnes in 1996 and forecast unless there is a serious disruption to supplies from Zaire the market will show a further small surplus of around 1,000 tonnes in 1997.
The above facts could see prices slip during the course of 1997, averaging $17 a pound for the year as a whole, Macquarie added.
Zaire which producers around 5,000 tonnes of cobalt continued to be eyed by traders. Reaction to the unrest spreading to the mineral rich Shaba region has so far been muted.

Low stocks and Japanese demand continued to drive indium higher. Several traders said prices had the potential to reach $400 a kilo near-term, while others said major producer China may release stockpiled material which would slow the rise.
Indium Corp of America moved its producer price higher by $25 a kilo to $315.
Elsewhere prices remained little changed.
Magnesium remained at steady levels, though some nearby tightness was noted.
